analysis.one_liner: Requires credit bureaus to get your permission before selling your credit report to lenders and insurers.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: it was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, credit bureaus like Equifax and Experian can sell your credit report to lenders and insurers unless you take action to opt out. This bill would flip that: the bureau would need your affirmative, verified consent before sharing your report for a loan or insurance application, and unsolicited credit and insurance offers could reach you only if you agreed. It would also bar the bureaus from charging consumers fees for managing this consent, require them to take real steps to prevent data breaches of your file, and direct the Government Accountability Office to study what further protections are needed. The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never received any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers gain control over who can see their credit report: no report could be shared for credit or insurance without their verified consent, they could opt in or out of prescreened offers at any time, and they could not be charged fees for exercising these rights. Their files would also get stronger protection against data breaches.

how_it_helps.text: Requires credit bureaus to get a consumer's affirmative, verified consent before sharing that consumer's credit file with lenders or insurers, instead of sharing by default unless the consumer opts out.
Lets consumers decide whether their name appears on the lists bureaus sell to companies making unsolicited credit and insurance offers, and to revoke that choice at any time.
Prohibits consumer reporting agencies from charging consumers any fees for these consent-related activities.

Requires credit bureaus to use commercially reasonable efforts to prevent unauthorized access to consumer files, and directs the GAO to study what further protections are needed to keep consumer data secure.

analysis.who_pays: Credit reporting agencies lose their default right to sell consumer files, and lenders and insurers lose easy access to prescreened prospects, facing new consent requirements and tighter data-security duties.

drawbacks.text: Requiring verified consumer consent before every credit pull could slow loan and insurance approvals and add compliance costs that lenders might pass on to borrowers.

The bill requires credit and insurance companies to obtain consumer consent for underwriting even for transactions the consumer initiates, a significant operational change for how credit checks have always worked under the opt-out system.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to consumers is real: control over who sees their financial data, fewer unsolicited offers, no fees for consent management, and stronger breach-prevention duties. The costs are real too: lenders and insurers would face friction in underwriting, and lenders argue prescreened offers widen access to credit; requiring verified consent before a report can be pulled for a loan could slow approvals and add compliance costs that may be passed on. The bill was never debated, so its practical design was never tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee when introduced, never received a hearing, vote, or floor action, and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on April 26, 2023, and read twice before being referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
No further action was ever recorded: the committee never reported the bill and the full Senate never voted on it.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and with it the bill, which would have had to be reintroduced from scratch in the next Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The credit bureaus and companies that buy consumer reports continue to operate under the existing opt-out system, selling consumers' credit files without needing their permission. Consumers keep the burden of protecting their own data.

for.name: Sen. Jack Reed
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and secured its referral to the Senate Banking Committee.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Democrats; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll calls or opposition positions were ever recorded.

industries.industry: Consumer credit reporting agencies (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion)
industries.note: The default permission to sell consumers' files to lenders and insurers would become opt-in, free of charge to consumers, with new duties to verify identity, honor consent changes within one business day, and prevent data breaches. Their core business—collecting and furnishing data on ordinary people without asking—would be substantially curtailed.

industries.industry: Banks, credit card issuers, and consumer lenders
industries.note: They could still pull reports with consent for a loan the consumer seeks, but prescreened unsolicited credit offers would require the consumer to opt in first. Firms that rely heavily on prescreen marketing would lose a channel for reaching customers.

Insurance underwriting would likewise require consumer consent, and prescreened insurance offers would be opt-in only. Firms that use credit reports to price policies and mass-market offers would lose access to consumers who never agreed.
